displayQuote: Hitch your wagon to a star

meta.title: Who really said "Hitch your wagon to a star"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuinely Emerson — verbatim in “Civilization” (Society and Solitude, 1870), and already in print in The Atlantic Monthly for April 1862.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Hitch your wagon to a star'?
meta.ogDescription: Really Emerson, word for word. But the date usually given (1870) is eight years late, and his argument was not about personal ambition.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Genuinely Emerson, word for word. The four words are a bare sentence on page 27 of “Civilization,” the second chapter of Society and Solitude (Boston: Fields, Osgood, & Co., 1870) — and the passage they belong to was already in print eight years earlier, in his essay “American Civilization” in The Atlantic Monthly for April 1862.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Society and Solitude: Twelve Chapters, ch. 2, “Civilization”
Boston: Fields, Osgood, & Co., 1870 — the sentence is on p. 27
“American Civilization,” The Atlantic Monthly, vol. IX, no. LIV (April 1862)
The London 1870 edition reads “waggon”; the Boston editions read “wagon”

source.excerpt: Gibraltar may be strong, but ideas are impregnable, and bestow on the hero their invincibility. “It was a great instruction,” said a saint in Cromwell’s war, “that the best courages are but beams of the Almighty.” Hitch your wagon to a star. Let us not fag in paltry works which serve our pot and bag alone. Let us not lie and steal. No god will help. We shall find all their teams going the other way, — Charles’s Wain, Great Bear, Orion, Leo, Hercules: every god will leave us. Work rather for those interests which the divinities honour and promote — justice, love, freedom, knowledge, utility.
trail: The full text of the 1870 Boston edition is on Project Gutenberg (eBook #69258) ↗, transcribed from Fields, Osgood, & Co., 1870; the sentence “Hitch your wagon to a star.” appears once, in the chapter “Civilization.”
We read the page image itself in the Internet Archive scan of that first American edition ↗ to fix the locator: the imperative is on p. 27, and the third-person form on p. 25.

The passage was in print eight years before the book. The April 1862 Atlantic Monthly (vol. IX, no. LIV) ↗ carries Emerson’s “American Civilization,” and its text runs sentence for sentence with the 1870 chapter through this paragraph — the third-person “to hitch his wagon to a star” is legible in the scan, and the imperative sits in the same position a few lines on, in a column whose scanned text is patchy. We read it there rather than inferring it.
Wikiquote’s sourced Emerson page ↗ also places the line in “Civilization,” which is the attribution most quote sites inherit.
source.excerptNote: The four famous words are a single sentence dropped into the middle of a paragraph about borrowing power from something larger than yourself. Two pages earlier Emerson writes the same image in the third person: “Now that is the wisdom of a man, in every instance of his labor, to hitch his wagon to a star, and see his chore done by the gods themselves.”

source.rightsNote: Both printings are comfortably in the public domain in the United States: the essay appeared in The Atlantic Monthly in April 1862 and the book in 1870, more than sixty years before the 1931 threshold. Emerson died in 1882. The text may be quoted, reproduced and reprinted freely.

author.name: Ralph Waldo Emerson
author.heading: About Ralph Waldo Emerson
author.bio: Ralph Waldo Emerson (1803–1882) was the central figure of American Transcendentalism, a former Unitarian minister who left the pulpit and made his living on the lecture circuit. Society and Solitude (1870) was assembled late in his career out of lectures he had been giving for years, which is why its sentences so often read like things meant to be said aloud — short, hard, memorable. He is one of the most quoted Americans in history and, partly for that reason, one of the most loosely quoted.

misattribution.heading: Real quote — but check the date and the meaning
misattribution.intro: Nobody else is being credited here: the words are Emerson’s exactly as they circulate. What travels wrongly is the date and, more often, the point.

items.why: Almost every quote site dates the line to Society and Solitude (1870), following Wikiquote ↗. But the paragraph it sits in had already appeared in Emerson’s “American Civilization” in the April 1862 Atlantic Monthly ↗ — eight years earlier. He recycled the essay into the book’s “Civilization” chapter, dropping the emancipation argument that had been its point and keeping the aphorisms.

Both are Emerson’s, two pages apart. The third-person version (“the wisdom of a man … to hitch his wagon to a star”) is on p. 25 of the 1870 Boston edition ↗; the bare imperative that became the saying is on p. 27.
The London 1870 edition ↗ prints “Hitch your waggon to a star” and heads the chapter “Civilisation” — a house-style difference, not a different sentence.

items.who: the “attach yourself to a rising star” reading
items.why: The line is often used as career advice — get close to someone successful and let them pull you along. In the paragraph it comes from, Emerson is arguing the opposite of self-advancement: the passage ends by telling the reader to work “for those interests which the divinities honour and promote — justice, love, freedom, knowledge, utility,” and warns that on paltry work that serves “our pot and bag alone” every god will leave us.

misattribution.truthLine: Verdict: really Emerson, verbatim — Society and Solitude ↗, ch. “Civilization,” p. 27 (1870), and in print by April 1862. Just don’t use it to mean networking.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Emerson is writing about technology, and the argument is stranger than the slogan. The paragraphs before this sentence marvel at watermills and tidal mills — machines that get their work done by borrowing the moon. That is his model for a well-lived life: don’t push, find the direction the enormous forces are already travelling and put your job in their path.

Then he makes the jump from engineering to ethics. If you can harness steam and gravity because they never swerve from their courses, you can harness principles the same way, because they don’t swerve either. “Hitch your wagon to a star” is the compressed form of that: pick work big enough that something larger than you is already pulling in its direction.
detailsBody: The essay had a political life before it had a literary one. “American Civilization” ran in The Atlantic Monthly in April 1862, in the middle of the Civil War, and Emerson used it to argue for emancipation. When he mined it for Society and Solitude eight years later, the war argument came out and the aphorisms stayed — which is how a wartime polemic ended up as one of the most-printed pieces of American self-help.
